hook: Egypt's showman pharaoh: warrior, builder, and maker of the oldest known peace treaty.

pages.x: Ramesses became pharaoh around 1279 BC, aged about 24, and reigned for 66 years. Most Egyptians alive when he died had never known another king. He had more than a hundred children and built a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, in the Nile Delta.

In 1274 BC he marched into Syria against the Hittites and walked into an ambush at Kadesh. By his own account he fought his way out almost single-handed. The battle was really a draw, but he had it carved on temple walls all over Egypt as a glorious victory.

Sixteen years later Ramesses and the Hittite king Hattusili III agreed to stop fighting and help each other against enemies. It is the oldest peace treaty whose text survives from both sides: in Egyptian hieroglyphs and on Hittite clay tablets. A copy hangs at the United Nations in New York.

In Nubia he had two temples carved into a cliff, guarded by four seated statues of himself, each 20 metres high. Twice a year the rising sun shines all the way to the back of the temple to light the gods inside. In the 1960s the temples were cut into blocks and moved uphill to save them from the waters of a new dam.

In 1976 his mummy was flown to Paris to be treated for a fungus. Egypt issued the long-dead king a passport, with his occupation given as "King (deceased)", and he was met at the airport with the honours due to a head of state.

Ramesses II was ancient Egypt's great builder and self-promoter, whose name is carved on more monuments than any other pharaoh. Nine later kings took his name, and to many people today he is simply "the pharaoh", often cast as the king in the story of Moses.
pts: Signed the oldest known peace treaty
